seo.title: Karmic tail 9 9 18 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 9 18 compatibility: two Hermits and the Moon. Why a couple that guards its quiet gets doubt as its task, read through the Odyssey and the cards.

title: The 9-9-18 karmic tail in compatibility: two cautious people and the Moon between them
short: The 9-9-18 tail in compatibility poses a riddle. The couple wants quiet and trust — The Hermit stands at the entry and again in the middle — yet the main task belongs to The Moon, the card of fear, guesswork and deception. The answer is this: nobody brings the Moon in. It grows out of the very quiet the two of them guard so carefully — in the dark between two lamps, each one fills in the other alone.

sections.h2: The Odyssey: the most cautious couple in world literature
paragraphs: Odysseus comes home disguised as a beggar and says nothing about who he is. Penelope talks with him by the fire at night as with a stranger. When it is all over and her husband stands before her without the mask, she sits down opposite him — and falls silent again. The subtlest trial of the poem is not the bow and not the suitors, but the question of who moved the bed.

Homer makes this couple equals in one quality: caution. Penelope's standing epithet is περίφρων — dictionaries give "very thoughtful, prudent"; Murray's English, as a rule, renders it "wise Penelope". The old nurse says Odysseus silenced her "in the great wisdom of his heart" (Zhukovsky's Russian makes him "cautiously wise"). In this couple both the husband and the wife are crafty, and the roles are not split by sex.

Set Waite's divinatory list for The Hermit beside them and it reads like a portrait of the pair. Upright it includes "Prudence, circumspection" and "dissimulation, roguery"; reversed, "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution". Dissimulation is Odysseus, who, in Homer's words, "made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth". Concealment is Penelope, who for three years wove a shroud by day and unravelled it by night. Disguise is the beggar's rags. Fear and unreasoned caution are Penelope at the hearth in Book 23.

Two Hermits in a couple's tail are not two lonely people. They are two people equally good at keeping their light to themselves. That is what makes them kin — and out of that same kinship grows their Moon.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a happiness only the two of them know (M = 9)
paragraphs: Cast up by the sea on a foreign shore, naked and with nothing, Odysseus wishes young Nausicaa the best thing he knows:
"For nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord, a great grief to their foes and a joy to their friends; but they know it best themselves."

Homer's word here is ὁμοφροσύνη, oneness of mind. The Greek of the last clause can also be read as "great fame for themselves", which is how Zhukovsky put it in Russian; Murray reads it as "they know it best themselves".

This is The Hermit at the entry to the task. The couple enters its task wanting a world that makes sense without explanations and needs no witnesses. Odysseus and Penelope have literally built such a world: a bedroom the husband raised in stone around a living olive tree, and a bed that, apart from the two of them, only one maid knows.

In everyday life it looks quiet. Friends hear about the engagement when the rings are already bought. A holiday means a cabin with no signal. An evening when each sits in their own armchair with their own book is not boredom for them but happiness. They love through deeds: they fix things, fetch things, remember that the other won't eat onions. Nothing is done in a rush — so much time passes between the first date and a shared flat that acquaintances stop asking.

In the couple's reading the same point also appears in the sphere "Relationship and common language": The Hermit is their common language. The two understand each other from half a word, and that is their gift. But in Lisovskaya's scheme the entry to the task lies on the line of tasks and can turn into resistance. Here the resistance is quiet: half a word starts to be enough every time, and each fills in the other half alone. A door closed to strangers one day turns out to be closed to each other's questions as well.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: twenty years, two fires (N = 9)
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of the tail has no meaning of its own — it is an addition to the main task; we read it as the path the couple takes from the wish to the task. Here again stands The Hermit, which means the path is walked alone, each with their own fire.
For twenty years Odysseus and Penelope live apart, and both survive by keeping secrets. He tells everyone he meets plausible stories about himself. She strings the suitors along with her loom:
"Then day by day I would weave at the great web, but by night would unravel it, when I had let place torches by me."

The most exact scene of the middle is the night in Book 19. Odysseus and his son carry the weapons out of the hall, and Athena goes ahead of them, unseen, "bearing a golden lamp". The son is amazed by the light, and the father cuts him short: "Hush, check thy thought, and ask no question". There is light, but you may not ask about it — the Hermit of the middle in a single line.

Then Penelope comes down into the empty hall and talks with the beggar by the fire deep into the night. She tells the stranger about her great ruse, the loom. He answers with fiction; Homer says he "made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth". She weeps for the husband who is sitting beside her; he pities her, yet "his eyes stood fixed between his lids as though they were horn or iron, and with guile he hid his tears." Two people in one circle of light — and each alone with their grief.

Benebell Wen offers two readings of The Hermit's light. The first is a light in the darkness for others. The second is a person "who sees the world through his or her own light", who "walks in the direction of his own thoughts only". When there are two Hermits, the second reading becomes the couple's plot: each sees the partner in their own light — and partly sees themselves.

Today this middle shows up in small things. One partner mentions being made redundant once the new job is already found: "I didn't want to load you with it." The other sorts out a hard conversation with their parents and reports it once it is settled. There are no loud rows — problems, as Lisovskaya writes of the Nine in its minus, pile up in silence. This is not coldness but care in The Hermit's language: you weather your storm yourself so as not to worry the other. The price is that the other learns of the storm only after it has passed — and starts wondering how many more there were. That thought is where the Moon begins.

sections.h2: Main task: recognising the person sitting opposite (D = 18)
paragraphs: The suitors are gone from the house, the nurse cries that the husband has returned, and Penelope comes down and sits facing him by the fire:

"Howbeit she sat long in silence, and amazement came upon her soul; and now with her eyes she would look full upon his face, and now again she would fail to know him, for that he had upon him mean raiment."

That flicker of "it's him — it's not him" is moonlight itself: now visible, now gone. Her son cannot bear it: "thy heart is ever harder than stone". Nor can Odysseus: "Strange lady! to thee beyond all women have the dwellers on Olympus given a heart that cannot be softened" — and he asks for a bed of his own: "that all alone I may lay me down, for verily the heart in her breast is of iron". Penelope replies: "Strange sir... right well do I know what manner of man thou wast, when thou wentest forth from Ithaca on thy long-oared ship."

Husband and wife address each other with one and the same word — in Homer it is δαιμονίη and δαιμόνιε, "strange one, past understanding". Each sees the other's coldness and not their own. And Penelope says the key thing about this couple's Moon task: **she is checking a living man against an image twenty years old**.

Lisovskaya, describing The Moon among a couple's tasks, names this too: an image created at the start that later collapses; feelings hidden because tenderness is taken for weakness. For a 9-9-18 couple the image is usually not false but out of date. The two change quietly, each on their own, and remember each other as they were. Years on, you can sit across from a person and measure them against who they once were.

In Waite there is a bridge between these cards. The reversed Hermit has "fear, unreasoned caution", and the reversed Moon has "Instability, inconstancy, **silence**". The silence two Hermits choose as peace already belongs, in Waite's list, to the Moon.
Where does the fear come from? Strangely, not from the partner. Before his homecoming Odysseus hears, in the land of the dead, the advice of Agamemnon, whose own return home ended in his death:
"Wherefore in thine own case be thou never gentle even to thy wife. Declare not to her all the thoughts of thy heart, but tell her somewhat, and let somewhat also be hidden."

And again: "for no longer is there faith in women." Penelope, explaining her coldness later, calls up Helen. Other people's marriages end up in this couple's bedroom. The Moon works the same way today: a friend's divorce, the parents' story, past relationships suggest the plot, and the partner answers for things they never did. Lisovskaya writes of jealousy and grievances spun from invented stories — here you can see where they are invented.

paragraphs.h3: Truth sent out through the gate of ivory

paragraphs: The subtlest clue is Penelope's dream. She dreams of an eagle that kills her geese and speaks with a human voice: "I, that before was the eagle, am now again come back as thy husband". She tells the dream to the beggar — that is, to Odysseus himself — and he confirms it: "in no wise is it possible to wrest this dream aside and give it another meaning". Penelope answers with a speech on the two gates of dreams: "one is fashioned of horn and one of ivory". Dreams through ivory "deceive men, bringing words that find no fulfillment"; those through horn "bring true issues to pass". And she decides her dream did not come through the gate of horn.

The truth has been said twice, plainly and aloud — and it is filed among the deceptions. Homer plays on words here: "ivory" (elephas) echoes the verb "to deceive" (elephairomai), "horn" (keras) echoes "to fulfil" (krainō). **This couple's Moon task is not only to stop believing phantoms but to recognise the truth when it is spoken simply.**

A detail that is easy to miss: in the same book Odysseus's eyes, holding back tears, are "as though they were horn or iron". The truth sits by the fire with eyes of horn and keeps silent. This is our observation, not Homer's gloss, but for the tail it fits: in a 9-9-18 couple the truth is more often not hidden but held behind a motionless face.

paragraphs.h3: A test is fear in disguise

paragraphs: The Moon also breeds a habit of testing. In the last book Odysseus comes to his old father in the orchard and hesitates "whether to kiss and embrace his father, and tell him all... or whether he should first question him, and prove him in each thing". He chooses the test, "to prove him first with mocking words". Just before, he had said outright what he feared: "see whether he will recognize me and know me by sight, or whether he will fail to know me, since I have been gone so long a time."

The one who tests is afraid of not being recognised. In a 9-9-18 couple the tests are small: will they notice I've been gone all evening; will they ask without prompting; will they remember without a hint. Each looks like caution, but at heart it is the question "am I still here for you?", asked in a way that makes it impossible to answer.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a room built around one trunk
paragraphs: The 9-9-18 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 31 — 3.26% of all date combinations, seventh of the 97 couple's tails. What stands next to it is more interesting.

The centre of the couple's matrix — the atmosphere inside the union — comes in only two kinds for these couples: The Moon in 74%, The Hermit in 26%. "The couple's values" are also only these two cards: The Hermit in 76.3%, The Moon in 23.7%. A third card never appears, and that is no coincidence. Adding and reducing numbers preserves the remainder on division by nine, and in any matrix the entry to the tail, by that remainder, equals the main task plus the centre. In this couple both the entry (9) and the task (18) divide by nine — so the centre must too, and among numbers up to 22 that leaves only 9 and 18. By the same arithmetic the couple's values must divide by nine as well.

**Five key points of this couple — the three cards of the tail, the atmosphere and the values — are written with two cards.** Like Odysseus's bedroom, built around one trunk: everything inward in this couple grows from the same olive. The Moon in the atmosphere of three couples out of four is the gift hidden in the task. According to Lisovskaya, in its plus such a couple understands each other by intuition and every year discovers something new in the partner. A partner who can never be known to the end is both an anxiety and the thing people hold on to for years.

A couple's tail is made from the partners' personal tails, and here there are only seven combinations. The most frequent are 15-5-8 + 21-4-10 (48% of these couples), 12-19-7 + 15-8-11 (24%) and 18-3-12 + 18-6-6 (17%). Our own run over the same dates adds a detail: in 82.3% of couples neither partner has The Hermit or The Moon in their personal tail, and in the remaining 17.7% both partners have these cards in their personal tails. It never happens that only one of them brings them.
In this couple there is no "hermit" and no "dreamer", no one who "shut down first". The quiet is made by two — as in Homer, where caution is shared equally.
The same 9-9-18 order also exists as a personal tail — for 924 dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points; the personal tail has an article of its own.

sections.h2: The bed of living olive: what disperses the Moon
paragraphs: Recognition does not come through evidence. The nurse has already seen the scar on her husband's leg — Penelope did not believe her. In Book 19 the beggar described Odysseus's cloak and golden brooch exactly — she believed he had seen her husband, not that he was her husband. Something else works. "So she spoke, and made trial of her husband": Penelope orders his bed to be carried out of the bedroom for him.
And the man with the motionless eyes flares up:
"Woman, truly this is a bitter word that thou hast spoken. Who has set my bed elsewhere?"

The bed cannot be moved: its base is the stump of a living olive around which he himself built the bedroom. In Murray's words, "a great token is wrought in the fashioned bed, and it was I that built it and none other." And at once Odysseus imagines the worst: "whether by now some man has cut from beneath the olive stump, and set the bedstead elsewhere."

This is a flash of jealous Moon — a story made up in a second. And it is exactly what proves to Penelope that her husband is before her: a stranger would not have flared up. Wen draws a precise line: "Key 2 is about disguise. Key 18 is about revelation of the inner self". Disguise belongs to another card; the Moon is the minute when the inner self comes out. **In a 9-9-18 couple the Moon gives way not when the evidence is in, but when someone stops holding their face still.**
Penelope answers in kind. "Be not vexed with me, Odysseus" — and for the first time she names her fear aloud:
"For always the heart in my breast was full of dread, lest some man should come and beguile me with his words; for there are many that plan devices of evil."
A fear said aloud stops being the Moon and becomes simply a fear, something two people can deal with together. "Lo, thou dost convince my heart, unbending as it is."

Then Homer gives a simile that seems to be the wrong way round. As shipwrecked men who swim to land are glad of the shore, "even so welcome to her was her husband, as she gazed upon him". It is not Odysseus who is compared to the shipwrecked, but the one who sat at home for twenty years. In a couple of two Hermits there is no "one who left" and no "one who waited": each went through their own shipwreck alone, and both need the shore.

And then "the long night she held back at the end of its course" — Athena delays the dawn. The Moon's time becomes a time for telling. Penelope speaks of the years in a house full of strangers. Odysseus tells of himself — and not only of what he endured: he "recounted all the woes that he had brought on men, and all the toil that in his sorrow he had himself endured". Earlier still, when he mentions a new and heavy prophecy, she asks him not to put it off: "come, tell me of this trial, for in time to come, methinks, I shall learn of it, and to know it at once is no whit worse." And he, the master of half-said things, answers: "Yet I will declare it, and will hide nothing. Verily thy heart shall have no joy of it". Two Hermits turn their light towards each other.

sections.h2: What changes the script: five habits instead of tests
paragraphs: Leaving the tail's script does not require becoming loud and sociable. Hermits stay Hermits; what changes is where they shine their light.

ul: **A sign instead of an exam.** A 9-9-18 couple shares much that nobody else knows: pet words, places, the story of how they met. That is their olive. Among the Moon's minuses Lisovskaya names a partner's secrets turned into weapons; the strong version of the tail makes shared secrets a root, not a weapon.
**Name the fear instead of testing.** Instead of "let's see if they notice" — "I'm afraid that…". A test is fear in disguise; said aloud, it loses its force.

**Tell before, not after the fact.** The storm need not be shared, but its coming can be announced: "I'm having a hard week, I'm coping, I'll tell you later." That is enough for the other not to fill in the rest.
**Check against the living person, not the image.** Now and then ask each other what has changed. Two Hermits change in silence, and the memory of the earlier partner ages faster than it seems.

**Distinguish withdrawing into yourself from withdrawing from the other.** Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Moon to accept that a partner's need to withdraw is a way to recover, not a lack of love. For two Hermits this is the main rule of quiet: silence frightens no one once it has been agreed on.

paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is Odysseus and Penelope at the end of Book 23: two people who went through everything alone and now stay awake until dawn because they are telling each other. "Nor did sweet sleep fall upon her eyelids, till he had told all the tale."

sections.h2: How the couple's tail is calculated: example 14.08.1975 and 14.10.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A person born on 14.08.1975 has the personal tail 15-5-8 and centre 7. A person born on 14.10.1975 has the tail 21-4-10 and centre 11.

paragraphs: The couple's middle is not derived from the two outer numbers: it is added up from the personal middles, 5 + 4. In this example The Moon also stands in "The couple's values" and in the point "What to create together" (8 + 10 = 18), while The Hermit also sits in "Common language". The couple's tail is read by its own roles: the partners' personal tails are not retold in it.

sections.h2: 18-9-9 and 9-18-9: the same cards in a different order
paragraphs: The same numbers make two more couple's tails. In 18-9-9 (1.754% of couples; The Moon in the centre for 57.1%, The Hermit for 42.9%) The Moon stands at the entry: the couple enters its task through enchantment, mystery and a shared fantasy, and the main task becomes The Hermit — not to drift into two separate cells and not to go cold.

In 9-18-9 (1.136% of couples; The Moon in the centre for 81.3%, The Hermit for 18.7%) The Hermit stands both at the entry and in the task, and The Moon in the middle: the path runs through a fog of misunderstandings, and the lesson is not to hide in one's shell. In 9-9-18 the order is the least noticeable: first comes the quiet, and the fog arrives at the end as its direct consequence.

**M · 9 The Hermit — "Entry to the task".** What the couple wants together: a world of their own with no audience, understanding without spare words, an unhurried pace. This is also their common language.
**N · 9 The Hermit — "Middle of the task".** How the couple walks towards the task: each with their own light, settling much alone and telling the other after the fact.

**D · 18 The Moon — "Main task".** What grows in that quiet: guesses, tests, the fear of being deceived, a memory of the partner in place of the partner. The lesson is to get to know each other again and again, and to say aloud what usually gets filled in by imagination.

intro: A couple's tail predicts nothing and passes no verdict on the union: it shows where the same difficulty keeps returning for the two of them. That difficulty has a great literary double. It is not a story of love at first sight but of a husband and wife who kept faith with each other for twenty years — and when they met again, could not open up.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-9-18 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, made of three cards. The Hermit at the entry: the couple wants quiet and a world of its own. The Hermit in the middle: the path is walked in silence, each with their own light. The Moon in the main task: guesses, tests and fears grow out of the quiet. The lesson is to get to know each other again and again, and to say aloud what usually gets filled in by imagination.

faq.q: Are the couple's tail 9-9-18 and the personal tail 9-9-18 the same thing?
faq.a: No. The couple's tail comes from adding up the points of two personal matrices, and its points mean the couple's entry, middle and main task. A personal tail with the same numbers occurs for 924 dates since 1900; it is a different calculation with different roles for the points.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: A couple's tail does not grade the union and predicts nothing. It shows where a difficulty keeps returning for the couple: here, in the silence from which guesses grow. The same two cards also give strength: deep conversations, respect for boundaries, the ability to keep discovering each other for years.

faq.q: Why does such a couple only ever have The Moon or The Hermit in the centre?
faq.a: It is the arithmetic of the matrix: reduction preserves the remainder on division by nine, and by that remainder the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With an entry of 9 and a task of 18 the centre can only be 9 or 18: The Moon in 74% of these couples, The Hermit in 26%.

faq.q: How can a couple find its own tail?
faq.a: Enter two dates of birth in the compatibility calculator: the reading shows the three cards of the tail in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail". By hand, add up the matching points of the two personal tails and reduce any sum above 22, as in the example above.

The couple's tail 9-9-18 — two Hermits and The Moon — is built like that scene. The couple enters its task through quiet, walks it in silence and gets The Moon as its main task: guesses, tests, the fear of being deceived. **Nobody brings the Moon in — it grows out of the very quiet the two of them guard so carefully.**

report.h3: A bed that cannot be moved

report: Recognition does not come through evidence: the nurse told of the scar, the beggar described the cloak and brooch — Penelope did not believe. So she orders his bed carried out of the bedroom, and the man with the motionless eyes flares up: "Who has set my bed elsewhere?" The strong version of the tail is two people who went through everything alone and now stay awake until dawn because they are telling each other.
